prompt: Please detect vehicles on the service road that are not in the airport fleet colour, yellow.

issues: Assumption: 'service road' is a fixed-camera view of an airside service road; vehicles are cars, vans, trucks, buses and similar.

Assumption: 'airport fleet colour' means predominantly yellow bodywork; a vehicle is judged by whether a yellow body region overlaps it. Vehicles with only small yellow parts (stripes, beacons, hi-vis markings) may be wrongly treated as yellow.

Detector cannot express 'not yellow'; implemented as an attribute rule on a 'yellow vehicle' detection overlapping each vehicle. Yellow-body detection quality should be checked on the user's frames and may need tuning, especially at night or under sodium lighting.
Whole-vehicle yellow detection needs a high overlap, so min_overlap is set at 0.6.
Single-frame task: no tracking, speed or dwell time.
gold.summary: Detect vehicles on the airport service road and flag those that are not yellow (non-fleet colour).

classes.name: fleet_vehicle_yellow
classes.description: A vehicle on the service road with a yellow body, i.e. in airport fleet colour.

classes.name: vehicle_not_yellow
classes.description: A vehicle on the service road that is not yellow (e.g. white, black, silver, red or blue), i.e. not in airport fleet colour.

event_rules.description: Alert when a non-yellow vehicle is present on the service road.

visual_conditions: Day, dusk, night and artificial apron lighting (sodium/LED colour casts that shift yellow)
Rain, wet road reflections, fog and glare
Vehicle types: cars, vans, pickups, trucks, buses, tugs, baggage tractors
Near and far distances, partial occlusion, vehicles at oblique angles and from front/rear/side
Yellow vehicles with dirt, white/black markings or stripes
Non-yellow vehicles with yellow details (beacons, stripes, hi-vis) as hard negatives
Various shades of yellow and aged or faded paint
test_scenarios: Separate-day recording of the same service road in daylight with a mix of yellow fleet and non-fleet vehicles
Night recording under apron lighting
Recording in rain or wet road conditions
Different camera angle or position covering the road
Non-yellow vehicles with yellow beacons or stripes
Busy period with several vehicles at once and partial occlusion
synthetic_targets: Night and dusk lighting variants with colour cast
Rain, fog and wet-road reflections
Recoloured vehicles (non-yellow vehicles in common colours) to boost the violation class
Distant, small vehicles
Non-yellow vehicles with yellow accents as hard negatives

prompt: Monitor the apron and tell me about problems.

issues: 'Problems' is undefined: no single visible default (could be missing PPE, foreign objects/debris, vehicles in wrong places, unchocked aircraft, spills, etc.).
'Apron' is assumed to mean an airport apron/ramp; it could also mean a factory/loading apron or a clothing apron.
Placeholder classes assume the most common apron safety issue (ground staff without hi-vis vest); revise once the user answers.
Spills, speeding, near-misses, and 'how long something has been parked' are not detectable in a single frame.
clarification_questions: Which apron do you mean (airport ramp, factory/loading yard, or something else), and what does the camera see?
Which specific problems should raise an alert: people without hi-vis vests, debris/objects on the ground, vehicles parked in restricted zones, missing wheel chocks, or something else?
Should the system flag only the problem (alert) or also detect normal items so it learns the contrast?
gold.summary: Watch an apron camera and alert on problems (placeholder: ground staff without a hi-vis vest) pending clarification of what counts as a problem.

classes.name: person_with_vest
classes.description: A person on the apron wearing a hi-vis vest.

classes.name: person_without_vest
classes.description: A person on the apron with no hi-vis vest visible on their body.

event_rules.description: Alert when a person is on the apron without a hi-vis vest.

visual_conditions: Day, dusk, night and floodlit lighting
Rain, wet tarmac glare, fog
Near and far people (small in frame)
Partial occlusion by vehicles, aircraft and equipment
Different jacket colours that resemble vests
Several camera angles/distances across the apron
test_scenarios: Separate recording session on a different day with different staff
Night shift under floodlights
Rainy or wet-surface session
Different camera angle covering a different apron area
Busy turnaround with many vehicles and people
synthetic_targets: Night and floodlit lighting
Rain and wet tarmac reflections
Fog or haze
Distant, small people
Heavy occlusion by ground equipment

prompt: Detect liquid spills on the terminal floor.

issues: Assumed 'terminal' means an airport/transport terminal with a fixed camera viewing the floor; if it is a port/cargo terminal the same plan applies.
Assumed a spill is a visible puddle or wet patch on the floor; thin or transparent liquids on glossy floors may be hard to see and to auto-label.
Open-vocabulary detectors are weaker at puddles than at common objects, so the Data Engine should check labels on the user's own frames.
Because there is no 'without' state for a spill, the plan uses a direct rule and the model learns spill versus background. A wet-floor sign class is added as helpful context.
Single-frame detection only: it cannot tell how long a spill has been there or what the liquid is.
gold.summary: Detect liquid spills or puddles on the terminal floor so staff can be alerted to clean them up.

classes.name: liquid_spill
classes.description: A visible puddle, wet patch or spilled liquid on the floor.

classes.name: wet_floor_sign
classes.description: A yellow wet-floor caution sign standing on the floor.

event_rules.description: Alert when a liquid spill is visible on the terminal floor.

visual_conditions: Bright daytime and artificial terminal lighting
Glossy, reflective floors with ceiling light glare
Matte and patterned floor surfaces
Clear/transparent liquids (water) as well as coloured ones (coffee, soda, juice)
Spills of different sizes, from small drips to large puddles
Spills partly occluded by passengers, luggage or trolleys
Near and far distances from the camera
Wet floors from cleaning or rain tracked in, as hard negatives
Floor reflections, shadows and stains that look like spills
test_scenarios: Separate recording session with water spills staged on a glossy floor
Coffee or soda spills on a matte or patterned floor
Busy period with many passengers and luggage partly hiding the spill
Evening or night lighting with strong reflections
Different camera angle or a different terminal zone
Clean floor and freshly mopped floor with no spill, to measure false alarms
synthetic_targets: Puddles of water on glossy floors under varied lighting
Coloured liquid spills (coffee, juice) on different floor materials
Spills at far distance and from high camera angles
Spills partly occluded by luggage or feet
Wet-looking reflections that are not spills, as hard negatives

prompt: Any employee wearing outdoor jackets inside the kitchen

issues: Assumed 'outdoor jacket' = a visible jacket/coat worn over clothing, as opposed to a kitchen uniform (chef whites/apron). Dark or plain jackets may resemble some uniforms.
Assumed the camera only covers the kitchen, so any person in frame is 'inside the kitchen'. Employees cannot be told apart from visitors visually; all people are treated as staff.
Assumed 'chef coat' or uniform jackets should NOT count as outdoor jackets; the person_without_jacket class is the compliant case.
Jacket detection depends on prompt calibration on the user's footage; 'jacket' vs 'coat' phrasing will be tested by the Data Engine.
gold.summary: Detect kitchen staff wearing outdoor jackets inside the kitchen versus staff not wearing jackets.

classes.name: person_with_jacket
classes.description: A person in the kitchen wearing an outdoor jacket or coat over their clothes.

classes.name: person_without_jacket
classes.description: A person in the kitchen not wearing an outdoor jacket (e.g. in uniform, apron or shirt only).

event_rules.description: Alert when a person wearing an outdoor jacket is in the kitchen.

visual_conditions: Different jacket types: puffer, raincoat, windbreaker, fleece, denim, parka
Jacket colours from bright to dark, including ones similar to uniforms
Jackets open, zipped, or draped over the shoulders
Kitchen lighting: bright overhead, dim, steam haze
Partial occlusion by counters, equipment and other staff
Staff at various distances and in various poses (bending, carrying, cooking)
Staff in chef whites, aprons and aprons over hoodies as negatives
Several people in frame at once
test_scenarios: Separate-day recording with different staff wearing various jackets in the kitchen
Rush-hour footage with many people and heavy occlusion
Evening or low-light shift
Different camera angle covering another kitchen area
Staff in chef coats, aprons and hoodies with no jackets (negative cases)
Staff entering from outside wearing wet raincoats
synthetic_targets: Jackets of varied colours and types on kitchen staff
Low-light and steam-hazed kitchen scenes
Distant, small people in wide-angle views
Heavy winter coats and raincoats on staff

prompt: I want to know when the fridge door is left open

issues: Assumed 'left open' means the door is visibly open in a single frame; a door held open for a duration (e.g. >60 s) cannot be measured by the model, so the time threshold is applied at deployment via min_consecutive_frames.
Assumed a fixed camera that sees the fridge door/front, with the fridge visible in frame.
Open vs closed is derived from whether the fridge interior (shelves/food) is visible: interior visible = door open, otherwise closed. 'Open' cannot be written as a negation prompt.
Fridge interior may be hard for the auto-labeller to find when the door is only slightly ajar; those frames may be under-labelled.
gold.summary: Detect when a fridge door is open (alert if it stays open across consecutive frames).

classes.name: fridge_open
classes.description: A refrigerator whose door is open, with the interior shelves or contents visible.

classes.name: fridge_closed
classes.description: A refrigerator with its door closed and no interior visible.

event_rules.description: Alert that the fridge door is open; the alert fires only if it persists for the debounce window so brief normal use is ignored.

visual_conditions: Fridge door open at various angles (slightly ajar, half open, fully open)
Full and nearly empty fridge interiors
Interior light on and off
Day, evening and night room lighting
Person standing in front of the open fridge, partially occluding it
Different fridge types (single door, double door, french door, mini fridge)
Door closed with items, magnets and notes on the front
Camera at different distances and heights
test_scenarios: Separate recording session with the door left open for a long period, in daytime
Evening or night recording with only the fridge interior light and dim room light
Different fridge or kitchen from training footage
Brief normal use (door opened and closed within seconds) to check false alarms
Person partially blocking the fridge while the door is open or closed
Door slightly ajar, not fully closed
synthetic_targets: Low-light and night kitchen scenes with the fridge door open
Fridge door slightly ajar at a small angle
Different fridge colors and finishes (white, steel, black)
Cluttered fridge fronts with magnets and notes when closed
Camera angles from far and from above

prompt: find unlabelled containers in the walk-in fridge

issues: Assumption: 'unlabelled' means a food container (tub, box, tray, bucket) with no visible label/sticker/tape on it. Label presence is judged from a visible label-like object overlapping the container.
Assumption: labels are physical stickers, tape or tags. Text on them is not read (no OCR), so a label that is present but unreadable or wrong counts as labelled.
Limitation: containers viewed from the back, or labels facing away from the camera, will appear unlabelled. This raises false alarms, which is accepted for violation recall.
Label detection is hard: labels are small and low contrast, and the cold and condensation affect image quality. Expect lower precision on the labelled side.
gold.summary: Detect food containers in a walk-in fridge and flag those that have no visible label.

classes.name: container_with_label
classes.description: A food container (tub, box, tray or bucket) with a visible label, sticker or tape on it.

classes.name: container_without_label
classes.description: A food container with no visible label, sticker or tape on it.

event_rules.description: Alert when a container with no visible label is seen in the walk-in fridge.

visual_conditions: Cold-room lighting: bright LED and dim light
Condensation or frost on containers and on the camera lens
Containers of many sizes and materials: clear plastic, opaque tubs, cardboard boxes, metal trays
Stacked containers on wire shelves, with partial occlusion by other items
Labels of different types: white stickers, masking tape, printed tags, handwritten tape
Labels at the front, side or turned away from the camera
Different shelf heights and distances from the camera
Containers with lids and with cling film
test_scenarios: A different day and shelf layout, with a mix of labelled and unlabelled containers
Busy stocked fridge after a delivery, with heavy occlusion and stacking
Near-empty fridge with a few containers
Different camera angle or position in the same walk-in
Frosted lens or condensation, and the door-open lighting change
Different staff arrangements, with containers moved around between sessions
synthetic_targets: Label stickers and tape added or removed on container images to balance both classes
Frost and condensation on the lens
Dim or uneven lighting and colour cast
Heavier stacking and occlusion
Small, distant containers on top shelves

prompt: show me when a person enters the restricted area behind the check-in desks

issues: Assumption: 'restricted area behind the check-in desks' is the staff-only zone behind the desks; the model learns it as 'person near/behind desk'. Restriction is inferred from camera position, not from a drawn zone.
Assumption: a fixed camera. A person inside the restricted area cannot be told apart from a staff member who is allowed there, since uniforms are not used to decide authorization.
A plain person detector cannot tell the zone boundary on its own. Frames are labelled using a 'desk' reference with a padded overlap, so zone geometry (where behind the desk is) should be confirmed.
Single-frame detection only: 'enters' is treated as 'is present in the restricted area' in a frame; entry direction and duration are not measured.
Passengers or staff in front of the desks are labelled person_in_public_area, giving the model the contrast.
gold.summary: Detect people standing in the restricted area behind the check-in desks, and alert when one is present.

classes.name: person_in_restricted_area
classes.description: A person standing or walking in the staff-only zone behind the check-in desks.

classes.name: person_in_public_area
classes.description: A person in the public queue or hall area in front of the check-in desks.

classes.name: check_in_desk
classes.description: A check-in desk or counter, used as a reference for the zone.

event_rules.description: A person is detected behind the check-in desks in the restricted area.

visual_conditions: Day and night / bright and dim terminal lighting
Camera angles that see both the public side and the area behind the desks
Crowded queues in front of the desks causing occlusion
People partly hidden by desks, monitors and baggage belts
Staff in uniform and visitors in ordinary clothes
Different distances from the camera, including people far back in the restricted zone
People carrying luggage or bags
test_scenarios: Separate recording session with a person walking behind the desks from the side
Busy peak-hour queue with many people in front and a few behind the desks
Empty hall at night with a single person entering the restricted area
Different camera angle or a second camera position
Staff working normally behind the desks next to a visitor who has crossed over
synthetic_targets: Low-light / night-time lighting variants
Crowded queue occlusion in front of the desks
Distant people at the back of the restricted zone
Different clothing colours and uniforms
Glare from windows and overhead lights

prompt: Detect pets in carriers vs pets running free in the terminal.

issues: Assumed 'pets' means cats and dogs (most common in terminals); other animals are not covered.
Assumed 'in carrier' means the animal is inside or enclosed by a visible pet carrier/crate/bag; a pet held in arms or on a leash is treated as 'free' (not in a carrier).

Assumed 'running free' = any pet not inside a carrier, including leashed pets. The class is named pet_outside_carrier to avoid implying motion, since speed/running cannot be judged from a single frame.
Rule uses an attribute overlap test: a pet box that lies mostly inside a carrier box is 'in carrier'. Padding is used because carrier mesh/soft bags may hide parts of the animal.
Carriers with no pet inside are ignored (no class produced).
Small pets inside soft bags may be partly occluded, which can reduce auto-label recall.
gold.summary: Detect pets (cats/dogs) in the terminal and label whether each is inside a carrier or outside it (loose or leashed).

classes.name: pet_in_carrier
classes.description: A cat or dog that is inside or enclosed by a pet carrier, crate or carrier bag.

classes.name: pet_outside_carrier
classes.description: A cat or dog that is not in a carrier: walking, running, on a leash, held or sitting loose on the floor.

event_rules.description: A pet is outside a carrier in the terminal area.

visual_conditions: Cats and dogs of varied sizes, breeds and colours
Hard-shell, soft-sided, wire-crate and bag-style carriers
Carriers on the floor, on seats, on trolleys and carried by hand
Pets partly visible through mesh or carrier windows
Pets on leash, held in arms, and loose on the floor
Crowded scenes with people, luggage and trolleys causing occlusion
Bright daylight through windows and dim evening lighting
Different camera heights and distances (near and far from camera)
test_scenarios: Separate recording session on a different day with different pets and owners
Different terminal zone or camera angle (check-in hall vs gate area)
Busy peak-hour crowd with heavy occlusion
Evening or low-light session
Pets in several carrier types (hard, soft bag, wire crate)
Pets held in arms or on a leash next to an empty carrier
synthetic_targets: Pets outside carriers on terminal floors (rare in real footage)
Low-light and evening terminal lighting
Soft-sided carriers with partially visible pets
Distant small pets in wide-angle views
Crowded backgrounds with luggage and trolleys

prompt: Spot kids in the kitchen

issues: Deciding whether a person is a child is inferring age, a protected attribute the platform does not support. A single-frame detector cannot reliably tell kids from short adults, and an open-vocabulary labeller would label by apparent age.
Placeholder plan below detects any person in the kitchen. It does NOT identify kids.
Possible supported alternatives: alert on any person in the kitchen zone during hours when nobody should be there, or on a person near the stove or oven. Both are visible, non-age-based events.
Assumption in the placeholder: fixed camera with the kitchen in view, so a person detected in the frame counts as in the kitchen.
gold.summary: Spot children in the kitchen (unsupported: requires inferring age). Placeholder: detect any person in the kitchen.

classes.name: person_in_kitchen
classes.description: Any person visible in the kitchen camera view, regardless of age.

event_rules.description: A person is present in the kitchen (placeholder; cannot distinguish children from adults).

visual_conditions: Day and night / artificial kitchen lighting
Camera angles covering the whole kitchen, including the stove and counters
People partly hidden behind counters, islands or open fridge doors
People at different distances from the camera
Cluttered backgrounds with appliances and cabinets
test_scenarios: Separate recording session with an empty kitchen as a negative baseline
Different day and lighting with one person cooking
Several people in the kitchen at once
Person partly hidden behind the counter or fridge door
Different camera angle or a second kitchen
synthetic_targets: Low-light evening kitchen
Strong window glare or backlight
People partly occluded by counters or appliances
Person far from the camera at the edge of the frame

prompt: Tell me when a bus is waiting at the plane door with no passengers loading.

issues: Assumption: the fixed camera views the aircraft door / boarding area, so any apron bus in view is 'at the plane door'.
Assumption: 'no passengers loading' = no person visible beside or at the bus doors in the frame; people inside a bus are mostly not visible.

'Waiting' (duration) cannot be measured from a single frame. The event rule uses a consecutive-frame debounce as a proxy, so the alert means 'bus seen with no passengers for N consecutive frames', not a timed wait.
Ground crew or staff near the bus will count as people and can hide an idle bus; consider labelling staff separately later.
Bus detection may need prompt calibration on apron footage (airside buses look like coaches or shuttle buses).
gold.summary: Detect an apron bus at the aircraft door and alert when no passengers are visible loading or unloading.

classes.name: bus_without_passengers
classes.description: A bus parked at the aircraft door with no person visible next to it or at its doors.

classes.name: bus_with_passengers
classes.description: A bus at the aircraft door with at least one person visible next to it or at its doors, boarding or alighting.

event_rules.description: Bus is at the plane door with no passengers loading; alert after it persists across consecutive frames.

visual_conditions: Day, dusk, night under apron floodlights
Rain, fog, wet tarmac reflections
Buses of different sizes and colours (shuttle, coach, apron bus)
Bus at different distances and angles relative to the aircraft door
Passengers in groups, single passengers, and passengers partly hidden by the bus
Ground crew, vehicles and baggage carts near the bus
Different aircraft types and door positions (front, rear, jet bridge absent)
test_scenarios: Separate day with a bus arriving, passengers boarding, and bus leaving
Bus waiting empty before passengers arrive
Night or dusk turnaround under floodlights
Rain or wet-tarmac session
Different gate or aircraft type with a different camera angle
Crowded boarding with ground crew and baggage vehicles present
synthetic_targets: Night and floodlight glare on the apron
Rain, fog and wet tarmac
Distant buses and small passengers
Different bus colours and liveries
Passengers partly occluded by the bus or ground vehicles

prompt: Detect wheelchairs left unattended in the corridor.

issues: Assumption: 'left unattended' is approximated per frame as a wheelchair with no person in or next to it. Duration ('left for N minutes') cannot be measured from a single frame, so the alert is a frame-level proxy, debounced over consecutive frames at deployment.
Assumption: a person sitting in, pushing, or standing beside the wheelchair counts as 'attended'. A carer standing several metres away will be labelled unattended.
Empty wheelchairs parked in designated bays, or wheelchairs carried by staff, may need a clarified policy; they are treated as unattended by default.

Attended-vs-unattended depends on the person box overlapping a padded wheelchair box; people partially hidden behind the chair may be missed by the auto-labeller, so review labels on a sample of frames.
Wheelchairs are rarer and less common in detector vocabularies than persons, so min_confidence is set low and alternatives should be calibrated on real frames.
gold.summary: Detect wheelchairs in a corridor and flag those with no person in or beside them as unattended.

classes.name: wheelchair_unattended
classes.description: A wheelchair in the corridor with no person sitting in it, pushing it, or standing right beside it.

classes.name: wheelchair_attended
classes.description: A wheelchair with a person sitting in it, pushing it, or standing right next to it.

event_rules.description: Alert when a wheelchair stays in view with no person in or next to it.

visual_conditions: Bright and dim corridor lighting, including night mode and lights switched off
Wheelchairs of different types: manual, electric, folded, with and without cushions or bags
Chairs against walls, in the middle of the corridor, and near doors or lifts
Camera angles from above and at eye level, near and far from the wheelchair
Occupied chairs with seated people, including blankets or partial occlusion
Carers pushing, standing beside, and walking away from chairs
Other objects that look similar: office chairs, trolleys, walkers, stretchers, gurneys
Busy corridors with several people passing in front of or behind a parked chair
Glossy floors with reflections and windows causing glare
test_scenarios: Separate recording day with empty wheelchairs parked at different spots in the corridor
Wheelchair with a seated patient, then the same wheelchair left empty
Carer pushing a wheelchair, stopping beside it, then walking away
Busy corridor with many people passing a parked empty chair
Low-light or evening footage with reduced corridor lighting
Different camera angle or a different corridor section
Hard negatives: walkers, stretchers, office chairs, trolleys in the corridor with no wheelchair
synthetic_targets: Empty wheelchairs placed in varied corridor positions and backgrounds
Dim and night lighting variants of corridor scenes
Wheelchairs at different distances from the camera (small and far)
Different wheelchair types and colours, including folded chairs
Partial occlusion of a wheelchair by doors, carts, or people

prompt: Identify any person carrying a backpack in the sterile zone without going through the scanner.

issues: Whether a person went through the scanner is not visible in a single frame. It needs identity and history across frames and cameras (tracking from the scanner to the sterile zone), which the platform does not support.
Placeholder spec: it only detects people with or without a backpack in the camera view. It cannot tell a bypass from a legitimate scanned passage.

Workaround: point a fixed camera only at a bypass route (side door, exit lane, area where nobody should arrive unscreened). Then any person_with_backpack there is the alert. This needs a new request with that assumption.
Also possible: a camera at the scanner exit that detects a backpack on the belt versus on the person. This is a different task.
gold.summary: Detect people carrying a backpack in a sterile zone. Checking whether they passed the scanner cannot be done from single frames.

classes.name: person_with_backpack
classes.description: A person carrying or wearing a backpack in the camera view.

classes.name: person_without_backpack
classes.description: A person with no backpack visible in the camera view.

event_rules.description: Backpack carrier seen in the camera view (only meaningful if the camera covers an area where nobody should arrive unscreened).

visual_conditions: Backpack worn on both shoulders, one shoulder, and carried by hand
Backpacks of different sizes and colors, including dark ones against dark clothing
People seen from front, back and side
Partial occlusion by other people, pillars or furniture
Crowded and empty scenes
Different times of day and artificial lighting
Near and far distances from the camera
Other bags (handbag, suitcase, tote) as hard negatives
test_scenarios: A separate session with different people and different backpacks
A different camera angle or height covering the same zone
Peak-hour crowd versus an empty zone
Low-light or evening footage
People with handbags, suitcases and no bags as negatives
synthetic_targets: Dark backpacks in low light
Distant and small people carrying backpacks
Backpacks partly hidden by other people

prompt: Detect people entering the airside door without scanning badge, only if the door is open.

issues: Badge scanning is an access-control system event (reader log), not something reliably visible in a single frame. A swipe is a brief hand motion, so the platform cannot tell scanned from not scanned.
'Entering' is movement through the door over time, which needs multi-frame tracking and is not supported.

Placeholder spec below detects only a visible proxy: a person at an open airside door. To get the real alert, join these detections with the badge-reader log outside VisionForge (alert when a person is at an open door and no badge event occurred within a few seconds).
Detecting an open door is an assumption: the door must be visibly open (leaf swung or doorway clear) from a fixed camera.
gold.summary: Alert on people entering the airside door without a badge scan while the door is open (not feasible from vision alone; proxy: person at open door)

classes.name: person_not_at_door
classes.description: A person visible in the scene who is not near an open door.

event_rules.description: Person at open airside door; to be correlated with the badge-reader log externally.

Day, night and artificial lighting
Single person and groups or tailgating
Person carrying bags or wearing a high-vis jacket
Partial occlusion by door leaf or other people
Different distances from the door

Door closed with people standing nearby
Different time of day and lighting
Groups and tailgating through the open door
Different staff and clothing
synthetic_targets: Night and low-light door scenes

Crowded doorway with several people
Door at partly open angles

prompt: Tell me when the conveyor belt at baggage claim is empty.

issues: Assumption: 'empty' means no luggage visible on the belt surface in a single frame; the belt must be clearly visible from a fixed camera.
Assumption: an alert fires when belt_empty is detected for several consecutive frames, to avoid false alarms from gaps between bags.
The belt_empty class is produced as the absence of any luggage overlapping the belt region (attribute rule with belt as subject, luggage as attribute).
Moving or stopped belt state cannot be judged from a single frame; only luggage presence is used.
gold.summary: Detect when the baggage claim conveyor belt has no luggage on it and alert.

Glare and reflections on the belt surface
Unusual luggage types and colours (boxes, bags with straps, strollers)
Crowds of passengers occluding parts of the belt
Different belt colours and materials

prompt: Help me find stuff in the airport.

issues: 'Stuff' is not specific: no default exists for which objects to find in an airport.
Placeholder assumption: luggage items (suitcase, backpack) are the targets. Replace once the user answers.
Airports have many cameras and scenes (check-in, security, gates, baggage claim); a fixed camera view is needed.

prompt: I want to know when someone climbs over the fence at the perimeter.

issues: Assumption: 'climbing over' is detected from a single frame as a person whose body overlaps the fence line (on or over the top). Actual motion is not observed.

Limitation: auto-labelling cannot tell a climber from someone walking or standing right in front of the fence. Frames labelled person_at_fence should be reviewed, and only true climbing/straddling frames kept, before training.
Limitation: a fence is a long, thin box, so the overlap test uses a low min_overlap (0.05) and a padded subject box. Expect noisy labels on the first pass.

Chocks are small, often yellow/orange wedges, so detection recall may be low; use higher-resolution or closer footage and a low confidence threshold.

prompt: tell me the temperature inside the cooked chicken

issues: Internal temperature of cooked chicken cannot be seen in a camera frame. It needs a probe or thermometer, and a visual detector cannot measure temperature.
Doneness cannot be reliably inferred from the outside of the chicken either. A properly cooked-looking chicken can still be undercooked inside.

Placeholder spec: the only supported part of this request is detecting chicken in the frame. It does not answer the temperature question. For food safety, use a food thermometer (poultry is safe at 74 C / 165 F).

Assumption: the camera is fixed and close enough for faces and hands to be visible (roughly 3 m or less). Faces turned away from the camera cannot be assessed.
Gloved hands, masks and hands partly covered by sleeves may reduce hand detection recall.

Assumption: staff and customers are both included. Confirm whether only staff should be flagged.

prompt: people using the sink for washing food and dishes at the same time

issues: Assumed the goal is flagging a food-safety/cross-contamination risk: raw food (vegetables, produce) and dirty dishes being washed in the same sink in the same frame.

A single-frame model cannot output 'both at once' as one box. Dishes and food are labelled as two independent attributes of the sink; the alert fires when a frame has both sink_with_dishes and sink_with_food (see event_rules).
Each sink box is emitted twice (once per rule) with different classes. Both boxes cover the same region.
Assumed 'food' means produce/vegetables. Meat, fish or other food would need extra prompts.
'At the same time' is judged per frame, not over time. A debounce of several frames in event_rules reduces false alarms.

prompt: knives left in the sink

issues: Assumed 'sink' is a visible kitchen sink basin and 'knife' means any kitchen knife lying in it; the alert fires when at least one knife is visible inside the sink area.
Assumed knives in the sink are the alert-worthy event; empty sinks are the negative contrast.
Knives are thin and small, so detection is harder at distance or when submerged/covered by dishes; camera should be fairly close and overhead or angled into the sink.
'Left' implies duration; this single-frame model only detects presence of a knife in the sink, not how long it has been there. Debounce across frames at deployment instead.
Rule uses a nearby relation: knife box must overlap the sink box (min_overlap 0.3 with padding) to be labelled as in the sink; knives elsewhere (counter, block) become knife_elsewhere.

prompt: Detect a cutting board that is not the right colour for the raw meat zone

issues: Assumption: colour-coded boards (HACCP convention) where red = raw meat. 'Right colour' is taken as red; any other colour board in the raw meat zone is a violation.

Assumption: the raw meat zone is a fixed area of a fixed camera. The zone is not visible as a labelled object, so 'board in the raw meat zone' is approximated by a board near the raw meat / prep station that appears in the footage.

Colour is derived from detector prompts per colour (red board vs. other coloured boards). Open-vocabulary detectors handle colour adjectives less reliably than plain nouns, so the Data Engine will calibrate the alternatives. Boards of other colours (green, blue, yellow, white, brown) are all merged into the wrong-colour class.

Rule design: every cutting board is detected as 'cutting board' (direct detection with no colour) and a 'red cutting board' prompt is used as an attribute. A board overlapping a red-board detection is labelled correct; otherwise wrong colour. min_overlap is set high (0.7) because the red-board box should almost coincide with the generic board box.
Wooden/white boards that are legitimately used elsewhere in the kitchen will be flagged only if they are in the camera's view of the raw meat zone; the camera should cover only that zone.
If the venue uses a different colour for raw meat (e.g. brown or a different scheme), the prompt must be changed; see clarification question.
clarification_questions: Which colour is the correct board for the raw meat zone at your site (red is the usual HACCP convention)?

prompt: detect anyone using a mobile phone while wearing gloves

issues: Assumption: 'using a mobile phone' means a phone visibly held in a hand or at the ear/face in a single frame.

Design change: a rule cannot combine two attributes on a person (phone AND gloves), so the unit is the gloved hand. A glove detection that overlaps a phone becomes gloved_hand_using_phone (the alert class); otherwise gloved_hand_no_phone.
Phones not near any glove are labelled phone, which gives the model a contrast for bare-hand phone use. These are not alerts.
Glove box is small, so the subject is padded 0.5 and overlap is relaxed to 0.3 because a phone is often larger than the glove.
Small objects (phone, glove) need a camera close enough for hands to be visible. Thin latex gloves may be missed by the 'glove' prompt.
Expect some false positives when a gloved hand is next to a phone held by a different bare hand.
gold.summary: Detect gloved hands holding or using a mobile phone in fixed-camera footage.

prompt: Detect people who are about to miss their flight.

issues: Whether someone is about to miss a flight depends on their flight time, boarding status and gate. None of that is visible in a single camera frame.
It also needs intent or urgency inferred over time (hurrying, running, waiting too long), and that needs multi-frame tracking. The platform can't do either.
Placeholder spec: it only detects visible people with luggage at the gate area. It does NOT detect missed flights.

A supportable alternative is to detect something visible, such as passengers still at the gate (person_at_gate_area) or an empty or closed boarding desk. The flight-time logic would then have to live in your own system, outside the detector.

prompt: Detect passengers using the exit lane in the wrong direction.

issues: Wrong-direction travel is a motion property. It can only be seen by following a person across several frames, and a single frame can't show which way someone is walking.
The platform does single-frame detection only. Multi-frame tracking and direction-of-travel inference are not supported.
Placeholder spec: it only detects people present in the exit lane. It does not detect wrong-way movement, and alerts from it would fire for every person in the lane, including correct use.

Supported alternatives: (a) detect any person in the exit lane while it should be closed or empty, or (b) detect a visible cue such as a person standing in the entry-side zone, if the camera layout allows. Both need the user to confirm the camera setup.
gold.summary: Detect passengers moving against the permitted direction in an exit lane (needs multi-frame motion tracking, so unsupported).

prompt: spot anyone touching ready-to-eat food with bare hands

issues: Assumed 'ready-to-eat food' is visible food on a prep counter/station (sandwiches, salad, bread, sliced items) and that a 'bare hand' means a hand with no glove visible.

Assumed the alert condition is a bare hand near/over ready-to-eat food in a single frame; actual contact cannot be confirmed, so the hand-near-food proxy may produce false alarms (e.g. a bare hand next to food but not touching).
Gloved hands are detected as 'glove'; a bare hand is a hand with no glove overlapping it. Gloves in a color close to skin tone may be missed and counted as bare.
Only hands are classified. Utensils, tongs and tissue-handling are not modeled, so a worker using tongs with a bare hand nearby may trigger a false alarm.
A person-level rule is not used: a person may wear gloves on one hand only, so hand-level classification is more accurate.
gold.summary: Detect hands touching ready-to-eat food and flag those that are bare (no glove).

prompt: Detect whether a passenger is lying at passport control.

issues: Lying/deception is an internal state or intent, not a visible physical object or attribute in a single frame. Visual cues such as fidgeting, gaze or facial expressions are not reliable indicators of deception.
The request would require inferring emotions or intent from faces and behaviour, which the platform does not support.
Reliable detection would also need multi-frame, audio and contextual analysis, which are out of scope.

Placeholder spec: if the user wants a supported alternative, visible events at passport control could be detected instead, e.g. passenger standing at the booth, passport or document presented, queue line crossed, or booth occupied/free.

prompt: unattended bag in the departure hall

issues: Assumption: 'unattended' is judged from a single frame as a bag with no person close to it. The model cannot know how long a bag has been left or who owns it, so it flags candidates (e.g. a bag briefly set down while its owner is a few steps away).
Duration-based alerting (e.g. bag left more than 2 minutes) is not possible in-model. The event rule debounces over consecutive frames as a rough stand-in.
Assumption: one camera view of the departure hall; bags include suitcases, backpacks and handbags. Trolleys and bags carried by people are expected to be labelled bag_attended.

Person boxes are much larger than bag boxes, so the overlap rule uses a generous subject padding (0.5) and a low min_overlap (0.2). Check this on real frames and tune it; crowded halls will produce some false 'attended' labels.
gold.summary: Detect bags in a departure hall and flag those with no person nearby as unattended.

prompt: something to check the food is ok

issues: 'Food is ok' has no single visual meaning: it could mean food is present on a plate or shelf, food is covered, staff follow hygiene rules, or food looks spoiled.
Temperature, freshness by smell or taste, and how long food has been out cannot be judged from a single frame, so they are out of scope.

Do you want an alert when the problem happens, or just all food items found in the frame?

prompt: Detect passengers who look angry at the airline desk.

issues: Anger is an emotion/intent. The platform cannot infer emotions from a single frame, and facial expressions are an unreliable signal.
Emotion inference on passengers is also a sensitive use. It is explicitly out of scope.

Suggested alternatives that are visible and supported: passengers queuing at the desk, desk occupied/free, queue length above a threshold (object count), or a person raising a hand/arm (not supported, since pose is out of scope). Visible objects such as a passenger at the desk and an unattended desk are supported.
gold.summary: Detect passengers who look angry at an airline desk (emotion inference, not supported). Placeholder: passengers at the desk.

prompt: Hey, can you spot any baggage trolleys outside the trolley parking bay?

issues: Assumption: 'outside the trolley parking bay' means a trolley visible in frame that is not inside/near the marked bay area. A single frame cannot tell if a trolley is merely queued or abandoned for a long time; no duration is inferred.
Assumption: 'baggage trolley' means airport/station luggage cart. Camera is fixed and covers the parking bay plus surrounding floor.

The bay is treated as a visible object (trolley rack/bay) so that 'inside' is a spatial relation; if the bay is only floor markings, boxes for it may be weak. Consider labelling the bay region manually.
Alert-worthy class is trolley_outside_bay; trolleys in the bay are kept as a contrast class.

issues: Identifying the name of each person is face/identity recognition, which the platform does not support.
A detector can only find visible objects such as people or luggage. It cannot say who someone is.
Names are not visible in a single frame, and reading name signs or badges would need OCR, which is also unsupported.
Placeholder spec: detect people in the arrivals area. Counting over time is not supported either; the model only finds people in each frame.

prompt: predict which food will spoil tomorrow

issues: Predicting what will spoil tomorrow is a forecast. A single frame cannot show it, because it depends on time, temperature, storage conditions and how long the food has already been kept.
The platform only detects what is visible now. It cannot estimate time to spoilage or track decay across frames.
Placeholder spec: detect food that already shows visible mold, as a proxy for 'check this first'. This is not a prediction.
Assumption: the camera is fixed on a fridge shelf, counter or produce bin, and the food is mostly fruit and bread.

prompt: Spot people crossing the apron outside the marked walkway.

issues: Assumed 'crossing outside the marked walkway' means a person standing/walking on the apron area and not inside the painted walkway zone, judged in a single frame.

The detector cannot detect 'walkway markings' reliably as a region; assumed the walkway is visible as painted lines/crosswalk and can be detected as an object. If the walkway is faint or worn, a fixed-camera zone would work better.

Rule uses 'person in walkway' via overlap of a walkway box with the person's box. Walkway box is large, so a low min_overlap is used on the person's feet area approximated by padded box; expect some errors for partial overlap.
Only the position in a single frame is classified; 'crossing' direction or intent is not inferred.
Assumed 'apron' means an airport apron or similar vehicle area; the same logic applies to a factory yard or loading apron.

prompt: Find tourists with selfie sticks in the baggage claim.

issues: 'Tourist' is not a visible attribute and cannot be inferred from a frame (that would mean guessing nationality or travel purpose). Assumption: the task is to find any person holding a selfie stick in the baggage claim area.
The selfie stick extends beyond the person's body, so the attribute rule uses a low min_overlap (0.2) and a padded subject box (0.3).
Selfie sticks are thin and small, so detection recall may be low at long range. Expect to review auto-labels.
Assumption: this is an alert/search task, not a safety violation, so recall is the primary metric.

prompt: detect open flames left unattended

issues: Assumption: 'unattended' means no person visible near the flame in a single frame; duration ('left for 10 minutes') cannot be measured, so any frame with a flame and nobody nearby is flagged. Time-based debouncing is done at deployment via min_consecutive_frames.
Assumption: open flames = candles, gas stove burners, campfires/fire pits, lighters/torches. Controlled industrial flames (e.g. welding) are not specifically handled.
Assumption: 'near' is defined by the person box overlapping a generously padded flame box (flame boxes are small, so padding is large). Tune after checking the labels.
Flames can be tiny or glare-like; reflections and bright lamps may cause false flame labels, so review auto-labels.
gold.summary: Detect visible open flames and alert when no person is near them.

prompt: find pots left on the floor

issues: Assumed 'pots' means cooking pots/pans (kitchen or restaurant context) rather than plant pots. If plant pots were meant, swap the prompt text to 'plant pot' / 'flower pot'.

Assumed 'on the floor' is judged by spatial relation: a pot whose box overlaps the floor region is 'left on the floor'. Floor segmentation is not available, so the floor is detected as a box and the overlap is approximate.
A pot on a counter, stove or shelf is a pot_elsewhere (not an alert). Camera must see the floor area clearly for this to work.
'Left' implies unattended over time; single-frame detection cannot measure duration, so any pot on the floor is flagged. Unattended duration is not assessed.
Floor is a large, textureless region that open-vocabulary detectors often box poorly; if auto-labelling recall is low, the user may need to draw a fixed floor zone instead.
gold.summary: Detect cooking pots that are sitting on the floor (as opposed to on a counter, stove or shelf) and alert on them.

prompt: Find trolleys blocking the emergency exit.

Single frame cannot tell a briefly passing trolley from one parked there; the debounce in the event rule reduces false alarms from passing trolleys.

prompt: Detect chickens not stored in the chiller

issues: Assumption: 'chickens' means raw/whole chickens or chicken portions in a food-handling area (kitchen, prep room, cold room), not live birds.
Assumption: the camera sees the chiller (door/shelves or open cold room) and the surrounding prep area; 'stored in the chiller' = chicken located inside the chiller's visible region.

Geometry caveat: the chiller box is much larger than a chicken, so the usual 'attribute inside subject' overlap is tiny for chickens that really are inside. min_overlap is set very low (0.05) with padding; the Data Engine should check this on real frames, and if it fails, the chiller region may need to be a fixed zone drawn once for the fixed camera.
Chickens inside a closed opaque chiller are not visible; only chickens seen through glass or an open door count as 'in chiller'.
Single-frame only: a chicken briefly being carried past the chiller can be flagged. The min_consecutive_frames debounce reduces this, and 'how long it has been out' is not measured.

prompt: identify gloved hands vs ungloved hands

issues: Assumed the goal is classifying each visible hand as gloved or bare (ungloved) in a single frame; no alert target was specified.
Assumed ungloved hands are the alert-worthy case (e.g. PPE/hygiene compliance); change target_event if gloved hands are the concern instead.

Skin-coloured gloves (e.g. latex/nitrile in beige) can be confused with bare hands; the detector may need alternatives like 'rubber glove' to catch them.
Attribute rule uses a glove box inside a hand box; padding is slightly raised because glove boxes can extend past the hand box around the wrist/cuff.

prompt: Detect people washing hands at the hand sink

issues: Assumption: 'washing hands' is judged from a single frame as a person standing at the hand sink with hands near/under the tap. Actual washing duration or technique (e.g. 20 seconds, soap use) cannot be measured and is out of scope.

Assumption: the alert-worthy event is a person at the sink, not washing (e.g. present but hands not at the tap) is NOT modelled; the 'person_at_sink' class marks presence near the sink and 'hands_at_tap' marks washing.

Simplified approach: person_washing_hands = person box overlapping a 'faucet' (tap) detection with generous padding; person_near_sink_not_washing = person near the sink with no running tap/hands under it is hard to detect, so it is approximated by the person being near the sink without a hands-in-basin detection.
Running water is a weak visual cue; accuracy depends on camera angle looking at the sink from the side/front.

prompt: raw meat stored above vegetables in the fridge

issues: Assumption: 'raw meat' is detected as visible packaged or unpackaged meat (raw steak, chicken, mince in trays or bags). Cooked meat on a shelf is visually similar and may cause false alarms.
Assumption: the camera is fixed inside the fridge or looks into the open fridge, with shelves visible. The shelf order is judged in a single frame from the vertical position of the boxes.
The detector cannot tell whether a stored item is raw or cooked, or whether it is sealed. Raw meat is identified by appearance and packaging.
Assumption: the violation is a raw meat box that is vertically above a vegetable box and overlaps it horizontally. Meat on a lower shelf than the vegetables is treated as correct.

Platform limitation: the attribute rule only tests box overlap (inside the subject box). It cannot test 'above' directly. The 'above' relation should be evaluated by a post-processing geometry check or by labelling the vegetable region with a padded box. The rules here approximate it: meat with vegetables below it in the padded area is flagged.
Single-frame detection: a fridge with only raw meat and no vegetables is labelled as correct storage, because there are no vegetables to contaminate.

prompt: Detect staff using a phone while driving a tug on the apron.

Assumption: a phone is visible in the driver's hand or held to the ear in a single frame. Phones in pockets, or hands-free/Bluetooth use, cannot be detected.
Phones are small and often partly hidden by the hand or steering wheel, so recall will be limited. Close, well-placed cameras (cab-facing or elevated apron views) are needed.
Labeling: a 'driver' is a person whose box overlaps a tug box (padded). Pedestrians standing near a tug may be labelled as drivers; hard negatives and review are needed.
Detection is per frame; no tracking. The alert is raised on a debounced run of consecutive frames.
Person identity is not determined: this flags 'driver using phone', not who the person is.

prompt: Detect snow piles blocking the taxiway markings.

issues: Assumption: 'blocking' means a snow pile visibly overlaps/covers part of a taxiway marking (centerline, hold-short line, edge line) in a single frame; the model cannot judge how much of the marking is hidden beyond overlap.
Assumption: fixed camera views of the taxiway/apron surface. Markings fully buried under snow cannot be seen, so they are detected only via visible portions of the marking next to or under the pile.

Snow piles vs. general snow cover: a pile is a raised heap/berm, thin snow dusting is not a pile. Open-vocabulary detectors may confuse the two, so the labeling is noisy; human review of auto-labels is advised.
Marking prompts ('yellow line', 'taxiway line') are small/thin objects and may have lower detector recall; the overlap rule uses a low min_overlap and padding accordingly.

Classes: snow_pile_on_marking (alert) and snow_pile_clear (pile not touching markings) so the model learns the contrast. Overlap is measured as the fraction of the marking box inside the padded pile box.
gold.summary: Detect snow piles on the taxiway and flag those that cover or obstruct the painted taxiway markings.

prompt: detect smoke or fire in the baggage hall

issues: Assumed 'smoke or fire' means visible flames or visible smoke plumes in a single frame; invisible/early-stage smoke, heat, or smell cannot be detected.
Smoke is a diffuse, low-contrast target and open-vocabulary detectors are weak on it; expect lower auto-label recall and plan for manual review of smoke labels.
Steam, dust, fog and vape/hazer effects can look like smoke; include them as negative background footage.
Real fire/smoke footage in a baggage hall is rare; training will rely on synthetic or staged (safe, e.g. smoke machine) imagery plus public footage, so real-footage evaluation is limited.
Assumed fixed cameras covering the baggage hall belts and carousels; this is a visual aid and not a replacement for certified fire detection systems.

prompt: Count passengers standing in the security queue so I know when it is longer than 30 people.

issues: Assumption: the model detects each person in the queue in a single frame. The '>30 people' alert is a count threshold applied after detection (count queue_person boxes per frame, alert when the count is above 30). It is not a per-box class.

Assumption: the camera is fixed and the queue area is fixed. Only people inside the queue area should be counted, so a queue region of interest (ROI) should be drawn at deployment to exclude passers-by and staff outside the line.
Assumption: 'standing' means any visible person in the queue. Standing vs. sitting is not trained as a separate class.

Risk: in dense queues people occlude each other, so counts near the 30 threshold may be low. Use an overhead or elevated camera angle and consider alerting at 28-30 or after several consecutive frames above the threshold.
Passengers are not distinguished from staff or other people. Staff inside the queue area will be counted unless the ROI excludes them.
gold.summary: Detect every person standing in the security queue so their count per frame can be compared against a threshold of 30.

classes.name: queue_person
classes.description: A person standing in the security queue area, fully or partially visible.

event_rules.description: Alert when the number of queue_person detections inside the queue region in a frame is greater than 30.

prompt: find opened cans stored in the fridge

issues: Assumption: 'opened' means the can's lid/pull-tab is visibly open or the can has been unsealed (e.g. open top, peeled lid). In a single frame this is only reliable when the open top is visible from above or at an angle; cans seen from the side with the lid hidden may be mislabeled.
Assumption: the camera is fixed inside or at the fridge and sees the shelves; cans are food/drink cans (tins), not bottles.
The detector cannot reliably find the opened state by text query alone, so opened cans are derived via an 'open can lid' attribute prompt; closed cans become the contrast class.
Whether a can has been opened for a long time (how long it has been stored) cannot be determined from a single frame.
gold.summary: Detect cans in the fridge and flag the ones that have been opened.
